claims.text: The initial material is a ferromagnetic high-entropy alloy based on transition metals such as Co, Fe, Ni, and Cu.
The initial alloy is disordered and has an FCC structure.
The initial alloy is equiatomic or near-equiatomic.
The untreated alloy has a modest intrinsic magnetocaloric effect.
Controlled nitriding can introduce interstitial nitrogen into the proposed alloy.
Magnetocaloric testing should be performed near the alloy's Curie temperature.
A controlled atmosphere during testing or processing will help avoid oxidation.
Nitrogen atoms will occupy interstitial sites in the alloy.
Interstitial nitrogen will induce lattice distortions.
Nitrogen-induced lattice distortions will modify local magnetic exchange interactions.
The modified magnetic interactions will produce a sharper or more favorable magnetic phase transition.
A more favorable magnetic transition will increase the magnetic entropy change during magnetization and demagnetization.
Nitrogen treatment will increase the magnetocaloric entropy change near the Curie temperature relative to the untreated alloy.
Nitrogen treatment may tune the transition temperature toward an application-relevant range.
Excessive nitrogen may form brittle or non-magnetic phases.
Brittle or non-magnetic phases formed at excessive nitrogen content may degrade magnetocaloric performance.
The magnetocaloric response may be sensitive to small compositional variations and processing conditions.

contradictions.description: The boundary explicitly anticipates detrimental phase formation only at excessive nitrogen content, which is compatible with an optimum at lower nitrogen content, but the falsification rule treats detrimental phase formation from excessive nitrogen as falsifying the overall hypothesis.
